title: What's the deal with MSG?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain monosodium glutamate (MSG): its natural occurrence in foods like tomatoes, cheese, oysters, and mushrooms; how it is now made by bacterial fermentation; the history of umami as the fifth taste discovered by Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 from kombu dashi; Ikeda's company Ajinomoto; gluten-free myth; the science on MSG safety, including injection studies and placebo-controlled trials; and the origin of the "Chinese restaurant syndrome" scare from a 1968 New England Journal of Medicine letter by Dr. Ho Man Kwok, later claimed as a prank by Dr. Howard Steele, which This American Life disproved. The episode closes with listener mail about a Chicago live show and a listener's update.

segments.title: Tour dates and opening banter about MSG in everyday foods
segments.summary: Hosts plug live shows, then riff on foods like nacho cheese Doritos, soy sauce, Maggi sauce, Vegemite, Accent, and oysters, noting that most people have eaten MSG without realizing it.

segments.title: What MSG is and where glutamate occurs naturally
segments.summary: MSG is monosodium glutamate, glutamic acid bonded to sodium. Glutamate occurs naturally in tomatoes, cheese, oysters, anchovies, mushrooms, potatoes, kelp, and breast milk. The FDA puts average glutamate intake around 13 grams per day, and added MSG around half a gram. The body does not distinguish manufactured from natural glutamate.

segments.title: Manufacturing MSG and the 1960s fear
segments.summary: Early twentieth-century production used propylene and acrylonitrile precursors. Modern MSG is made by bacterial and yeast fermentation of starches and sugars. Fermentation wastewater is hard to treat and can create dead zones. Excitotoxin claims are introduced.

segments.title: Umami discovery by Kikunae Ikeda
segments.summary: Recap of the five basic tastes. In 1908 Kikunae Ikeda isolated glutamate from kombu dashi and named the meaty taste umami. Glutamic acid had been identified earlier by Carl Ludwig RittHausen in 1866. Ikeda and Saburosuke Suzuki Jr. founded Ajinomoto, now a major MSG producer.

segments.title: Gluten myth, Escoffier, and using MSG in cooking
segments.summary: MSG is not made from wheat gluten; the name glutamic acid came from wheat gluten used in its isolation. Chef Auguste Escoffier used savory stocks and Maggi sauce. MSG is usually sold premixed with salt or seasoning because only small amounts are needed.

segments.title: Scientific evidence on MSG safety and placebo effect
segments.summary: The FDA says MSG is generally recognized as safe, which is not an absolute guarantee. Dietary glutamate does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier. Symptoms reported at about 3 grams in a single meal, six times average daily intake. Early injection studies in animals were poorly designed. Later double-blind tests found placebo produced the same symptoms.

segments.title: Origins of Chinese restaurant syndrome and the Kwok letter
segments.summary: Survey data show many Americans avoid MSG. Claims about MSG and obesity, appetite, and low-sodium products are discussed as unresolved. Dr. Ho Man Kwok's letter to the New England Journal of Medicine described symptoms after Chinese American food, sparking a racist media frenzy and the term Chinese restaurant syndrome. Dr. Howard Steele later claimed the letter was a prank, but This American Life found Kwok was real and the claim was false.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh gives Chicago show details and an update on a listener who relocated to Charlotte. A listener named Veronica writes about a Chicago live show and the community it created. The hosts sign off with mail contact information.
